How does Lasers laser? How does laser only burn bad stuff?

(this is a grossly oversimplified answer, but essentially correct)

Yes, the laser only burns bad stuff, just like your microwave heats some items faster than others.

Lasers, and microwaves, put out energy at a single frequency. Molecules respond to that energy at different rates; in the microwave, foods that contain a lot of oil will heat up more quickly because oil molecules absorb energy at the particular frequency the microwave is generating better than water will absorb energy at the same frequency. That's why you have hot and cold spots in your food when you nuke it (and why the walls of the microwave are barely warm even when you have been cooking for the last ten minutes).

Lasers work the same; the rust/corroded limestone/whatever will absorb energy (and resultingly flake away/burn to ash/vaporize) much faster than the uncorrupted material underneath. It's like the hot and cold spots in your food, just more dramatic.

A laser must be on a particular frequency to work this way; any laser won't work with every material. A laser used to remove rust from steel may be useless for removing corrosion from bronze, or paint from your car. It may destroy the bronze or sheetmetal on the car and leave the corrosion or paint intact. So going out and buying a random laser won't earn you big bucks in the restoration business, you'll spend a lot of money for a limited use.

How does Lasers laser?

They create alot of light of a particular wavelength then pass it through a bunch of filters until it's all vibrating exactly the same way (coherent).

How does laser only burn bad stuff?

The bad stuff is partially detached from the surface of the good stuff and is mostly surrounded by air, which is a poor conductor of heat, so it heats up faster and vaporises. It also help that stuff like rubber and paint has a lower boiling point than steel.

The good stuff is a solid piece of steel, which conducts heat quite well, so the heat applied to a particular spot radiates out over the whole piece quicker so the heat doesn't build up as quickly where the laser is shining. This is why processor heat sinks use a piece of metal to conduct heat away from the chip rather than just blowing air over it.

If they kept the laser concentrated in the same spot for too long it would heat up the good stuff and begin to melt/vaporise it.
